title: Q4 — policy objects vs scattered keys

sections.title: P7-Q4 — policy objects vs scattered keys
sections.text:
**Query:** Answer in prose, no tables. Why wrap several related configuration
keys (for example impersonation enabled, require-approved-by, max session
lifetime, read-only HTTP methods) into one immutable policy object injected
into middleware, instead of each middleware calling config() for four keys?
Contrast with a generic Options bag. Cite Fowler encapsulated context/policy,
Microsoft options pattern, Laravel middleware docs. Name primary-source URLs.

**Status:** success

Inject a small immutable policy object when those values jointly define one
authorization decision. Middleware then depends on “the impersonation rules”
rather than four configuration paths. Laravel resolves middleware from the
container and allows constructor type-hinting.

Scattered `config()` calls couple middleware to exact key names, coercion,
defaults, cross-field rules and the timing of reads. A policy constructed once
from one validated snapshot is seen by every method in the request. Fowler:
an object bundles data with behavior and establishes a common context.
Microsoft Options pattern: related settings are read through an options type
with validation. An Options bag answers “what were the configured values?”
A policy object answers “what rule applies?” Start with typed options at the
infrastructure boundary; promote to a policy when values interact, require
cross-field validation, or have several consumers.

Do not wrap a single feature flag used once. Do not build a mega-Application
Options object from unrelated tunables.

Primary sources: https://martinfowler.com/bliki/FunctionAsObject.html ·
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/options ·
https://laravel.com/docs/13.x/middleware

[листинг сокращён: ImpersonationPolicy vs четыре config() в middleware]

sections.title: P7-Q5 — blocking composition gate
sections.text:
**Query:** Answer in prose, no tables. Architectural fitness functions that
fail CI when a forbidden API such as Laravel config() is called outside an
allow-list of composition-root files (service providers, console commands).
Why must the gate include a planted negative test that names the offending
file? Contrast observational (warn, exit 0) versus blocking (exit 1). Cite
ThoughtWorks fitness-function-driven development, Pest PHP arch testing.
Name primary-source URLs.

**Status:** success

A CI rule forbidding `config()` outside composition-root files is an
architectural fitness function: it turns “configuration is wired at the edge”
into an automated integrity check. ThoughtWorks: fitness functions belong in
delivery pipelines.

The gate must include a planted negative test that puts `config()` in a known
forbidden file and asserts CI fails while naming that exact file. Without it,
green CI is ambiguous: the glob may have narrowed, the parser may miss helper
calls, exclusions may be too broad, or the job may not invoke the gate. The
planted violation proves fixture discovery → detection → diagnostic →
non-zero status.

Observational mode reports and exits 0; useful while measuring debt, but it
does not preserve the boundary. Blocking mode exits 1 and is the governing
force. A practical rollout is observational, then block new violations, then
remove the baseline. Keep the planted test in every phase. In blocking mode
it must demonstrate detected, named, and non-zero exit.

Pest Arch is strong for namespace/class rules. The literal helper `config()`
is often a token/AST scan. Run that scanner from Pest or as its own CI
command; what matters is the planted offender and the path-bearing message.

Primary sources:
https://www.thoughtworks.com/en-us/insights/articles/fitness-function-driven-development ·
https://pestphp.com/docs/arch-testing
